title: SODOM’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN YOU WERE TOLD — AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY ALL OF US
paragraphs: SODOM’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN YOU WERE TOLD — AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY ALL OF US

Why does the Bible condemn Sodom for sexual wickedness AND for pride, abundance, complacency, and abandoning the poor—and what happens when Christians only preach the half that condemns somebody else?
There is something deeply uncomfortable about the way the Bible talks about Sodom.
Not because Scripture is unclear.
Because Scripture may be clearer than we want it to be.
We have learned how to say “Sodom” and immediately think about somebody else.
Someone else’s sexuality.
Someone else’s rebellion.
Someone else’s lifestyle.
Someone else’s sin.
And then Ezekiel walks into the room.
And suddenly the finger we were pointing begins to tremble.
Because God says something about Sodom that many Christians have read dozens of times without allowing it to interrogate them.
Listen carefully.
“Behold, this was the iniquity of thy sister Sodom, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness was in her and in her daughters, neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.”
That is Ezekiel 16:49 in the KJV.
Now look at the Hebrew:
הִנֵּה־זֶה הָיָה עֲוֹן סְדֹם אֲחוֹתֵךְ גָּאוֹן שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט הָיָה לָהּ וְלִבְנוֹתֶיהָ וְיַד־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה׃
The words are devastating.
עֲוֹן — avon — iniquity, guilt, perversity.
גָּאוֹן — ga'on — pride, arrogance, exaltation.
שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם — siv'at-lechem — fullness, abundance, satiety of bread.
עָנִי — ani — poor, afflicted.
אֶבְיוֹן — evyon — needy, destitute.
God looks at Sodom and sees a society swollen with abundance while vulnerable people remain unsupported.
Full tables.
Empty compassion.
Comfort without mercy.
Prosperity without responsibility.
People who had enough to become generous...
and instead became proud.
But do not stop reading.
That would be just as dishonest as ignoring verse 49.
The next verse says:
“And they were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away as I saw good.”
Ezekiel 16:50.
That matters.
The Bible does not permit us to erase Sodom’s sexual wickedness in order to turn the story exclusively into a lesson about poverty.
And it does not permit us to erase Sodom’s arrogance, prosperous self-indulgence, violence, and neglect of the vulnerable in order to turn the story exclusively into a weapon against sexual sin.
God gives us the whole indictment.
We do not have permission to edit His evidence.
Go back to Genesis 19.
Two angelic visitors enter Sodom. Lot receives them into his house. Then the men of the city surround that house and demand that the visitors be brought outside so they can “know” them.
Whatever modern argument someone wants to attach to the chapter, the immediate scene is horrifying.
This is not romance.
It is not mutual affection.
It is threatened sexual violence.
It is domination.
Humiliation.
Predation.
A mob attempting to use human bodies as instruments of power.
And the New Testament refuses to let us pretend sexual rebellion is irrelevant to Sodom.
Jude 7 says:
“Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh…”
The Greek is even harder to dodge:
ἐκπορνεύσασαι … ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας
ekporneusasai … opisō sarkos heteras.
The first term describes giving oneself over to sexual immorality. The latter expression literally concerns going after “other” or “different flesh.”
So when somebody says, “Sodom had nothing to do with sexual sin,” Jude will not cooperate.
But when somebody says, “Sodom was only about sexual sin,” Ezekiel will not cooperate either.
Maybe that is the point.
We keep trying to make Sodom small enough to use against our preferred enemies.
God keeps making Sodom large enough to expose us.
Sexual corruption was there.
Pride was there.
Violence was there.
Exploitation was there.
Abundance without compassion was there.
Neglect of the poor was there.
Haughtiness before God was there.
These were not competing explanations.
They were branches growing from a diseased root.
Human beings had rejected God's order so profoundly that other people ceased to be neighbors to love and became objects to consume, ignore, exploit, dominate, or discard.
And suddenly Sodom is not safely buried beneath ancient ruins anymore.
It is standing frighteningly close to us.
Because what happens when a culture becomes sexually unrestrained while simultaneously becoming obsessed with itself?
What happens when bodies become commodities?
What happens when pornography trains human beings to consume one another?
What happens when the powerful exploit the vulnerable?
What happens when churches can thunder about sexual morality while stepping over desperate people?
What happens when Christians defend biblical sexuality but ignore biblical generosity?
What happens when people preach compassion while redefining whatever sexual boundaries God has established?
Different compromises.
Same terrifying instinct.
We want the parts of God's holiness that expose other people and quietly negotiate with the parts that expose us.
That is why Ezekiel 16 should make comfortable Christians uncomfortable.
Imagine sitting at a table overflowing with food while somebody outside cannot eat.
Imagine having three closets of clothes while another human being is shivering.
Imagine knowing someone is drowning financially, emotionally, spiritually—and having the ability to strengthen their hand—but saying, “Someone else will help.”
Then imagine opening your Bible and thanking God that you are not like Sodom.
Ezekiel whispers:
Look again.
This is where Scripture becomes personal.
Perhaps you have never joined a mob outside Lot's door.
But have you become proud?
Perhaps you would never defend sexual violence.
But have you secretly consumed another person's body through pornography?
Perhaps your theology of marriage is completely orthodox.
But does the poor person matter to you?
Perhaps you condemn immorality loudly.
But are you sleeping with someone who is not your spouse?
Perhaps you serve the poor faithfully.
But have you begun using compassion as permission to call something good that God calls sin?
Perhaps you can quote every verse about sexuality.
But when was the last time your abundance became somebody else's answered prayer?
That hurts.
It is supposed to.
Not because Jesus delights in crushing sinners.
Because Jesus loves sinners too much to leave our favorite hiding places undisturbed.
And here is where the story becomes infinitely greater than Sodom.
Because if Scripture only exposed us, every one of us would eventually stand condemned.
The Bible's message is not:
“Find the Sodomites and destroy them.”
The Gospel's message is:
“All have sinned.”
You.
Me.
The sexually broken.
The sexually proud.
The greedy.
The self-righteous.
The adulterer.
The porn addict.
The religious hypocrite.
The wealthy person who has forgotten mercy.
The activist who has forgotten holiness.
The preacher who secretly believes his correct doctrine makes repentance unnecessary.
The church member who knows exactly which sins God hates—as long as they are somebody else's.
We all need the same Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal collides with grace.
Jesus does not rescue us by pretending sin is harmless.
He rescues us by bearing its judgment.
At the cross, Christ does not redefine darkness as light.
He enters the darkness.
He carries guilt.
He bears wrath.
He sheds His blood.
He dies.
And on the third day, He rises.
The Gospel is not God lowering His holiness until sinners can comfortably climb over it.

The Gospel is the holy Son of God coming down to sinners, taking upon Himself the judgment His people deserved, and rising victorious so that those who repent and believe can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and transformed.
That means there is hope for sexual sinners.
Real hope.
Not affirmation that leaves us unchanged.
Grace that transforms us.
There is hope for the greedy.
There is hope for the proud.
There is hope for people enslaved to pornography.
There is hope for adulterers.
There is hope for people carrying sexual histories they cannot bear to remember.
There is hope for people whose desires have become their identity.
There is hope for wealthy hearts that have forgotten the poor.
There is hope for religious people who discovered that their morality had become pride.
There is hope for the person reading this who quietly thought:
“If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Jesus already knows.
Every room.
Every search.
Every touch.
Every fantasy.
Every selfish purchase.
Every person you ignored.
Every secret.
Every excuse.
Every night you promised God it was the last time.
He knows the scandal.
And the breathtaking announcement of Christianity is that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the grave because Christ is calling you into life.
Grace is not permission to remain what sin made you.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy meeting you in the wreckage and beginning to make you new.
Maybe that is why Sodom still matters.
Not so Christians can carry its name around like a stone to throw.
But so all of us can recognize what happens when human beings dethrone God.
Sex becomes detached from holiness.
Prosperity becomes detached from generosity.
Power becomes detached from mercy.
Desire becomes detached from obedience.
Comfort becomes detached from responsibility.
Religion becomes detached from repentance.
Eventually everything becomes about us.
My body.
My money.
My comfort.
My truth.
My appetite.
My life.
My rules.
And Jesus confronts the kingdom of self with two words that sound terrifying until you realize they are the doorway to freedom:
Not your appetite.
Not your bank account.
Not your political tribe.
Not your shame.
Not your sexual history.
Not your self-righteousness.
Me.
Jesus.
This is why Christians must refuse the false choice between holiness and compassion.
We do not have to choose.
Christ commands both.
We can uphold God's design for sexual holiness while loving sexually broken people with extraordinary tenderness.
We can care fiercely for the poor without pretending material generosity cancels rebellion elsewhere.
We can speak truth without cruelty.
We can show mercy without rewriting truth.
We can call sin “sin” because Christ offers forgiveness.
And we can call grace “grace” because forgiveness was purchased at an unimaginable price.
The cross leaves no room for superiority.
Nobody stands beneath it bragging.
Nobody arrives there because his sins were more respectable than his neighbor's.
We arrive empty-handed.
And perhaps that is the question Sodom finally asks us.
Not merely:
“What was their sin?”
But:
“What is mine?”
Where have I become proud?
Where has abundance made me numb?
Whose hand could I strengthen but have refused to strengthen?
Where have I violated God's sexual holiness—in action, imagination, consumption, secrecy, or desire?
Where have I used somebody else's sin to distract myself from my own?
Where am I asking Jesus to be Savior while resisting Him as Lord?
Sit with it.
Because sometimes the verse that makes you most uncomfortable is the verse God uses to open the prison door.
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But if you want to mark a moment of repentance, comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If shame has kept you hiding from Christian community, comment, “No more hiding.”

And if Christ has already pulled you from a place you thought you would never escape, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded believer from giving up tonight.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, repent honestly, heal biblically, and follow Jesus more faithfully, stay close by following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen—to follow as well.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue.
Keeping Gospel-centered resources moving outward takes real support.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Christian giving must be voluntary. Paul says giving is not to be done “grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if financial support is not possible for you, please do not carry shame.
Pray.
Those actions can help truth travel farther than you may ever know.
Because the goal was never to build an audience that merely says, “Amen.”
The goal is to make disciples who look more like Jesus.
People who are sexually holy and radically compassionate.
People who refuse both self-righteousness and moral compromise.
People whose tables are open.
Whose hands strengthen the weak.
Whose bodies belong to Christ.
Whose money belongs to Christ.
Whose sexuality belongs to Christ.
Whose influence belongs to Christ.
Whose wounds are being healed by Christ.
Whose sins are being confessed to Christ.
Whose lives increasingly say:
Jesus is Lord.
Maybe you opened this article expecting to discover what was wrong with Sodom.
Maybe God used it to ask what is happening inside you.
That is not the end of the story.
That may be exactly where grace begins.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the secret browser history.
Bring Him the coldness toward the poor.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the theology you used as camouflage.
Bring Him the years you cannot undo.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish had never happened.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Because the most terrifying thing about Sodom is not that ancient sinners became exceedingly corrupt.
It is how easily we can recognize their sins everywhere except in ourselves.
And the most beautiful thing about Jesus is that when He finally exposes what we were hiding, He is still mighty enough to save.
The sin you finally stop defending may become the very place where you discover how desperately you needed grace.
